materials.name: Painted plasterboard on studs
materials.notes: 12.5 mm board on a stud frame with a cavity. The board itself flexes, which is why the 125 Hz figure is the highest in the set — an ordinary partition wall is a mild bass absorber.

materials.name: Plaster on masonry
materials.notes: Solid and reflective at every frequency — no cavity to flex, so no low-frequency help at all.

materials.name: Thin wood panelling on battens
materials.notes: Ply or T&G over an air gap works as a panel absorber, taking more from the low end than the top.

materials.name: Lath and plaster
materials.notes: Older construction: springier than plasterboard, so a little more absorbent low down.

materials.name: Suspended mineral ceiling tile
materials.notes: 15 mm tile in an exposed grid. Broadband but shallow — it does little below 250 Hz.

materials.name: Thin carpet on a hard floor
Thick pile carpet with underlay
materials.notes: About as much high-frequency absorption as a floor can give — and still almost nothing at 125 Hz, which is the whole problem with treating a room from the floor up.

materials.name: Wooden floor on joists
materials.notes: A suspended timber floor flexes, so it takes a useful amount out of the low end.

materials.name: Laminate or engineered board on concrete
Single glazing
materials.notes: A single pane is light enough to move with the air, which makes it a surprisingly effective — and completely uncontrollable — bass absorber.

materials.name: Open doorway (nothing in it)
materials.notes: A hole. Sound that leaves through it does not come back, so it behaves as total absorption — the most absorbent thing a wall can have in it, and the reason a room measures differently with the door open.

materials.name: Solid core door
materials.notes: Heavy enough not to flex much: close to a wall acoustically, and what you want between a studio and the rest of the house.

materials.name: Glazed door
materials.notes: Mostly glass, so mostly reflective — and it reflects at exactly the frequencies a first reflection does its damage at.

materials.name: Triple glazing
materials.notes: Heavier than double, so it flexes even less: reflective right down the band.

materials.name: Cloth-upholstered seating
materials.notes: A fabric sofa or armchair. Standard published figures for cloth-upholstered seats, quoted per square metre of the floor the piece stands on rather than per square metre of its own surface. In a domestic room a three-seater in this covering does more above 500 Hz than a wall of thin panels, which is why leaving furniture out makes a room read far livelier than it is.

materials.name: Leather-covered seating
materials.notes: The same piece in leather rather than cloth. Standard published figures for leather-covered seats, per square metre of floor covered. Noticeably less absorbent on top than fabric, and the difference is audible in a small room.

materials.name: Lightly upholstered seating
materials.notes: A thinly padded seat over a hard frame, as against a deep cushioned one. Standard published figures for slightly upholstered seating, unoccupied, per square metre of floor covered. Close to nothing at the bottom, which is the honest way to model a hard dining chair with a pad on it.

materials.name: Seating with someone in it
materials.notes: Lightly upholstered seating, occupied. Standard published figures, per square metre of floor covered. Worth having because a room full of people measures very differently from the same room empty; use it to model the listening session rather than the empty studio.

materials.name: Light curtain over glazing, hung flat
materials.notes: An unlined curtain of about 340 g/m² hung straight and flat against the glass, which is how most domestic curtains actually hang. Barely touches the room below 500 Hz — what it does is take the top off. Standard published figures for light velour, 10 oz/sq yd, hung straight in contact with the wall; a class figure rather than a measurement of any one curtain.

materials.name: Medium curtain over glazing, gathered
materials.notes: A lined curtain of about 475 g/m² gathered to roughly half its flat width and spaced off the glass. Standard published figures for medium velour, 14 oz/sq yd, draped to half area; a class figure rather than a measurement of any one curtain.

materials.name: Heavy curtain over glazing, gathered
materials.notes: A heavy lined curtain of about 610 g/m² gathered to roughly half its flat width and spaced off the glass. The cheapest way to make a window behave, and reversible when the room needs to be live again. Standard published figures for heavy velour, 18 oz/sq yd, draped to half area; a class figure rather than a measurement of any one curtain. Fullness matters more than weight — the same fabric hung flat does a fraction of this.
